name: Zane Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've got lectures Monday to Thursday, and the rest of the week is hustle. I mow lawns and clean gutters for about a dozen neighbours on weekends, and I buy and resell trainers online in the evenings. I share a flat with two lads from my course, and my parents pay about half my costs.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My dad is a self-employed builder and he's always said, work for yourself and you answer to nobody. I wanted a skill that would let me do that, and software is the best one I could see. I got in with average results, but I make up for it by working harder than people who are cleverer than me. I use AI tools every single day: to write code, to price my trainers and to write my adverts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it saves me time but it's not a miracle. I'd tell people in my course that the ones who use it well still get ahead. Online I'd keep posting my deals, since that's the real business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's fine. The world carries on, there's still plenty of money to be made, and I'd be in the same race as everyone else. It's up to me, and I like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the lawns and the trainers, and I'd add a small website for my gardening service. I'd put thirty percent of my earnings into an index fund. And I'd look for an internship in year two with a small firm where I'd learn more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Confident. This is the world I'd bet on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still be a worry in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much, to be honest. My dad's building jobs are lumpy, so some months money's tight at home, and I'd feel I should help. But I earn enough to cover myself, which is my main goal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your trainer business dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch to something else, like reselling old laptops or fixing people's computers. I'm good at spotting what's under-priced. The thing is to keep your eyes open and your costs low.

say: I'd say it saves **time** but isn't a miracle, and people who use it well get ahead.
I'd keep posting my deals online.
think: The world carries on and there's plenty of **money** to be made.
It's up to me, and I like that.
do: Keep the lawns and trainers and build a small **website** for my gardening service.
Put thirty percent of my earnings into an index fund.
feel: I feel **confident**, since this is the world I'd bet on.
S0.quote: The thing is to keep your eyes open and your costs low.
fieldNote: Truly **calm**: self-employed habits and daily AI use fit this world.
Only mild worry is his father's lumpy building income.
Has quick fallbacks, like reselling old laptops.

steps.text: Build a small website for his lawn and gutter service
Put thirty percent of earnings into an index fund
Apply for a year-two internship at a small software firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's a great time to be building things. I'd tell my flatmates to use the tools more and moan less. Online I'd post what I've built with AI, because that gets noticed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think it's more chance than risk for people like me. Companies cut junior coders, but a person who uses AI can do the work of three and build their own thing. The ones who ignore it will get squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a tool for local trades, like a quoting app for builders, since my dad would be the first customer. I'd test it with ten small firms and charge a small monthly fee. And I'd keep studying, because the degree still opens doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit impatient, to be honest. I want to get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the risk for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I spread myself too thin and my grades drop. I'm already at average level, and some firms still check them. I'd have to keep a floor of at least decent marks, even while I hustle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a classmate who is worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say stop reading headlines and build one thing this month. Fear is quiet when you're busy. I know it sounds blunt, but it's what worked for me.

say: I'd say it's a great time to **build** things, and I'd tell flatmates to use the tools more.
Online I'd post what I've built with AI.

Test it with ten small firms and charge a small monthly fee.

steps.text: Build a quoting app for small builders like his dad

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment, and people who move first win. But I'd also say governments should be careful not to crush business with panic rules. I'd say it online and in the flat, loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my degree loses most of its value in two years, since AI does what I'm learning. The hands-on side lasts until about 2031, which means my dad's building work lasts longer. I'd have to bet on myself, not on a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd quit worrying about grades and put everything into the business. I'd turn the quoting app into a real product and sell it to builders, using my dad's contacts. I'd also put all the savings into the business and nothing into holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, and wired. It's like standing on the start line with the engine running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years' warning change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I need money coming in before my degree is worth nothing. I'd work double on the lawns and trainers this summer and sell the app early, even if it's rough. Waiting for it to be perfect would be fatal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him that builders using AI to quote and plan will win the work, and the ones who don't will lose it. He'd say he's too old to learn, and I'd say I'll do it for you. Robots on site are three years behind, so he's got a window.

I'd say it loudly online and in the flat.
think: My degree loses most of its value in two years, so I'd bet on **myself**, not a certificate.

S2.quote: Waiting for it to be perfect would be fatal.
fieldNote: Fear shows as **hurry**: he sells the app rough and early.
Gambles his savings on the business, which is a real risk.
Takes a deal with his dad: he'll learn AI for him.

steps.text: Sell the rough quoting app to ten builders using his dad's contacts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good run-up, and people should start now. I'd say less regulation and more training, because business adapts quicker than government. I'd tell my mates to stop waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate in 2029, with a few years of business behind me. I think the thinking AI will make entry jobs rare, but I'll have my own customers. The robots for hands-on work come around 2034, so my dad's trade lasts a good while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and run the business alongside it. I'd hire a classmate to help with the app and take a placement at a software firm. I'd invest part of my profits and keep part as cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A little uneasy, maybe, about the unknowns. But mostly ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's room to do things properly. With two years I'd rush and burn my savings, but with five years I can build slowly, hire help and keep the degree as a backup. It's the difference between a sprint and a long race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle, who drives a lorry. If robots take over driving around 2034, he's exposed. I'd tell him now to learn something else, and I'd say I'll hire him if I can. He'd laugh, but I'd mean it.

I'd tell my mates to stop waiting.

steps.text: Hire a classmate to help build and sell the app
Take a placement at a software firm in year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so get building. I'd say it online and to my family, and I'd say don't wait for someone to hand you a plan. People who take work and risk will do fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'd be 28 and I'd have a business, maybe two. The thinking AI would be part of the toolbox. I'd probably be hiring people by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and grow the business, and keep buying and selling small things for cash. I'd save for a house deposit and put money in shares. I'd try new AI tools the moment they come out, because that's how I stay ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Great, honestly. Excited and relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A recession, or my business idea failing. If the ten years became six, I'd have less time to build. I'd keep a cash buffer, six months of costs, so I can survive a bad patch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently starting now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be more careful with money. I spend too much on stock before I've sold the last lot. I'd keep a simple spreadsheet and learn the tax side, which no one tells you about until it's late.

I'd say people who take work and risk will do fine.
think: By 2036 I'd have a **business**, maybe two, and thinking AI would be part of the toolbox.
I'd probably be hiring people by then.
do: Finish the degree and grow the business while keeping a six-month cash **buffer**.
Save for a house deposit and put money in shares.
feel: I feel **excited** and relaxed, and honestly it feels great.
S4.quote: I spend too much on stock before I've sold the last lot.
fieldNote: Fully **calm** with ten years: his self-employed habits are an advantage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be fine in the end, but two years doesn't give time to build properly, and my dad and uncle would be caught short. What would help is light rules, tax breaks for small firms, and cheap training for older workers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as sure of myself as I sound. I put on a confident face, because that's how my dad taught me. Truth is I worry about letting the family down.

headlineQuote: I'm not as sure of myself as I sound. I put on a confident face, because that's how my dad taught me.
portrait: Zane is an **18-year-old** computer science student who mows lawns and resells trainers online while his dad builds houses.
He is traditional on family and free-market on money, and uses AI tools every day.
He sees **opportunity** first, builds apps and side businesses, and keeps a cash buffer.
He is calm in most scenarios and anxious only when the warning is two years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because there's no time to build properly and his dad and uncle would be caught short.
whatWouldHelp: Light **rules**, tax breaks for small firms and cheap training for older workers.
